Common Council moves controversial Elm Street housing project to next step in review process

by Brian Crandall August 21, 2026August 21, 2026

Share this:

  • Share on X (Opens in new window) X

Instaread

The City of Ithaca’s Common Council gave the green light Wednesday for a contentious apartment complex proposal to flesh out its concept plan and schedule public information sessions.

Stay informed with The Ithaca Voice!

Get our top stories delivered right to your inbox at 5 a.m. weekdays.

We will never share your information with anyone.

The proposal, planned for Elm Street in the City of Ithaca, would transform vacant wooded land adjacent to the Lehman Alternative Community School (LACS) into a 75-unit apartment complex made up of five buildings. The proposal would be its own apartment complex separate from the neighboring Whispering Woods Apartments  — formerly known as Chestnut Street Apartments.

It’s the first project to go before the Common Council after the body approved allowing any project in the city to apply for specialized zoning through a process known as a Planned Unit Development (PUD).

A PUD requires the direct approval of Common Council, giving the city’s elected officials a say in the project and adding an extra political layer that isn’t normally a part of the planning process.

The plans for the apartment complex increased in size following the urging of Common Council in June to create a denser, larger project for the property.

About 15 speakers came before Common Council Wednesday night to discuss the planned housing development for Elm Street.

Some of those in attendance spoke favorably about the plans. Tompkins County Housing and Community Development Director David West, a city resident, described the site as an excellent choice for multifamily development due to its proximity to schools and bus lines, and that the walk-up apartments and proposed traffic improvements were well-designed. 

City resident John King said that the development would have a lower carbon footprint than sprawling housing lots in the outlying towns. 

But plenty of speakers came before the council to oppose the project. George Ygarza, a resident of the Whispering Woods apartment complex, questioned whether the proposed units are family-friendly., He expressed concerns that the apartments would be poorly maintained, citing tenant issues with the management of Whispering Woods.

Longtime local environmental advocate Sarah Hess stated that more multifamily housing was inappropriate for West Hill, where the neighborhoods are characterized by single-family homes and several existing apartment complexes, such as the West Village Apartments and Cedar Creek Apartments. 

Several speakers cited concerns about traffic congestion on Elm Street. According to a 2025 study, the intersection of Floral Avenue, Hector Street and Elm Street is the fifth most dangerous roadway in Tompkins County.,   

A few of those who spoke before council sought a sort of middle ground. Katrina Davis, whose family recently bought a home on West Hill, supported development but also asked the council to ensure that fair community benefits were obtained in exchange for allowing the PUD. Elm Street resident Miranda Pagan was supportive of the multifamily housing proposal, but expressed concern that the project would create too much additional traffic on Elm Street. 

Of the speakers on Wednesday, older, longtime residents — many of whom said they have lived on West Hill for several decades — tended to be opposed to the proposal. The speakers who viewed the project more favorably tended to be younger.

Mayor Robert Cantelmo said that there will be multiple opportunities for public comment on the plans over a period of several months. A PUD zone and the project itself must both be approved by Common Council, as well as undergo environmental review by the City of Ithaca Planning & Development Board. He added that public information sessions would be scheduled if the PUD to allow multifamily uses is deemed acceptable in concept by council.

L. Bear Smith of HOLT Architects led the project team’s latest presentation before council. He noted that the buildings were broken up into smaller footprints rather than a single “bar shape.” 

“We specifically chose this building typography because it was the smallest footprint that we could possibly get. We could break it up into chunks, to allow more strategic placing with the topography,” Smith said. “Our goal is to try to position those buildings as strategically as we can […] to not have to clear cut everything. Our goal is to minimize impact.”

Whitham Planning and Design’s Jacob von Mechow said the project can still change in response to comment,  calling the project’s form and design a “first pass,” noting that there would likely be revisions between now and an approved final product. 

Following public comment, some members of council had reservations. Fifth Ward Alderperson Margaret Fabrizio had stormwater and traffic concerns, and asked if it would be possible to buy land from the school district to build a street connection to Chestnut Street. Fabrizio later added she couldn’t support a PUD at this time because she had not been presented details on what the apartments’ rents would be.

Third Ward Alderperson David Shapiro cited a public comment that LACS students currently use the wooded property to “decompress.” While the school district doesn’t own the property, Shapiro said he wanted to ensure a more substantive benefit for the students. Cantelmo later suggested a natural space or “grotto” might be more beneficial than a playground.

Many of the concerns expressed by council members will be answered by future studies in the planning process. Traffic studies are expected as part of site plan review and project review by the Common Council, and potential stormwater facilities and tree replantings would also be discussion items. 

The plans are general at this point, and are dependent on Council’s willingness to support the idea of the PUD before studies and analyses are paid for and undertaken, and finer details are resolved.

“A lot of my constituents have a lot of concerns about this. I really want to make sure that the democratic process is respected here, and I know we’re going to do our best to do that,” Shapiro said.

First Ward Alderperson Jorge DeFendini, who represents the area where the project is proposed for, pushed for two public information sessions, approaching TCAT to put in a bus stop to serve the development, and designating parking spaces for Ithaca Car Share vehicles. He also said he wanted educators and students at LACS to be engaged in the project as well.

DeFendini asked the developers if they could explore creating rough plans of what it would look like if the development was consolidated in three buildings instead of five, and if it was feasible to build a bridge over the creek near the Whispering Woods apartments to connect the two complexes. 

With all the additions and requests — as well as a second public information session — the vote to approve the PUD as a concept and schedule the first public information session passed 8-1 with Fabrizio opposed.
